analogy.p: Think of a recycling plant that receives rubbish (dead organisms and waste), sorts it and breaks it down into raw materials that factories (plants) can use to make new products. The faster the machines run (the warmer the temperature, up to a limit) and the better supplied they are with power (oxygen) and water for processing, the more material is processed each hour. If the machines overheat they break down (enzymes denature) and the plant stops. The analogy breaks down because a real plant has a fixed capacity, whereas decomposer populations grow in number when conditions are good, so the whole 'plant' gets bigger.

bullets: Decomposers are **microorganisms** (bacteria and fungi); they feed by secreting digestive enzymes outside their bodies (extracellular digestion).
Examples of material that decays: dead leaves, dead animals, faeces, food waste, milk.
Decay turns complex organic compounds (proteins, carbohydrates, fats) into simpler molecules, carbon dioxide and mineral ions.
Decomposition makes **biomass** from dead material available to other living things again.
Without decay, dead matter would accumulate and the nutrients locked in it would not be available to plants.
Decay depends on the activity of enzymes inside and outside the decomposers, so it follows the same rules as other enzyme-controlled reactions (temperature, pH, water).
core.h: What decay is and why it happens
core.p: **Decay** (decomposition) is the breakdown of dead plants and animals, and of animal waste, by **decomposers**: mainly **bacteria and fungi** (microorganisms), and also detritus feeders such as earthworms and maggots that break material into smaller pieces. Decomposers secrete **enzymes** onto the dead material which digest large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones, which they then absorb. They use some of these products for growth and for **respiration**. Decay is essential in ecosystems because it recycles the materials that living things are made from.

bullets: Carbon: dead organic matter --> decomposers --> CO2 (by respiration) --> plants use it in photosynthesis.
Minerals: nitrate ions are needed by plants to make **proteins**; magnesium is needed for **chlorophyll**.
Plants (producers) take up the ions; consumers get them by eating; decomposers return them.
If decay is slow, nutrients stay locked in dead material and growth of plants may be limited.
Fertilisers (natural such as manure and compost, or artificial) replace ions removed when crops are harvested, since the crop is taken away instead of decaying on the spot.
Link to the carbon cycle note: decomposers are the part of the cycle that deals with dead organisms and waste.
core.h: Why decay matters: recycling carbon and mineral ions
core.p: Decay returns **carbon dioxide** to the atmosphere, because decomposers respire as they break down dead material, completing the carbon cycle. It also returns **mineral ions** such as nitrates, phosphates and magnesium to the soil, where plants can absorb them through their roots. Plants need these ions to make proteins, DNA and chlorophyll, so decay keeps soil fertile. In a stable community the materials taken out of the soil by plants are balanced by those returned by decay, so the cycles are in balance.

bullets: **Temperature**: warmth increases the rate (more kinetic energy, more frequent successful collisions between enzymes and substrate, faster growth of microbes). Above the optimum, enzymes **denature** and the rate falls.
**Water**: moisture is needed for microorganisms to grow and for enzymes to work; very dry material decays slowly; waterlogged material lacks air.
**Oxygen**: aerobic decomposers need oxygen for aerobic respiration; without it decay is slower and different microbes act (anaerobic decay).
**Surface area / size of pieces**: small pieces have a larger surface area to volume ratio so decomposers act faster.
**pH**: strongly acidic or alkaline conditions slow decay by affecting enzymes.
The **type of decomposer** and the **type of material** also affect the rate (for example, some plant materials such as lignin decay slowly).
core.h: Factors affecting the rate of decay
core.p: The rate of decay depends on the conditions that affect the **decomposers**. Decay is quickest at a warm **temperature**, with plenty of **water** and **oxygen**. These are the conditions in which the decomposers' enzymes and respiration work best and in which the microorganisms grow and reproduce fastest. Gardeners and farmers try to provide these optimum conditions to speed up decay in compost heaps. When conditions are cold, dry or lack oxygen, decay is slower.

bullets: Rate increases with temperature up to the optimum because of increased collision frequency.
Beyond the optimum, **denaturation** changes the shape of the active site: the substrate no longer fits.
Denaturation is **irreversible**; do not say the enzyme is 'killed' (enzymes are not alive).
Freezing and refrigeration slow decay but do not usually stop all microorganisms; heating (pasteurising, cooking) kills many microbes.
On a graph of rate against temperature expect a **bell-shaped curve** (rise, peak, fall).
Higher tier thinking: describe the rate as a gradient on a graph of amount of decay against time.
core.h: Why the rate of decay changes with temperature (link to enzymes)
core.p: As temperature increases from a low value, the rate of decay increases because the particles have more energy and so collide more often and with more energy; microorganisms also grow and reproduce faster. There is an **optimum temperature**, often around 40 degrees C for many decomposers, at which the rate is highest. Above this, the shape of the **active site** of the enzymes changes and they are **denatured**, so substrates no longer fit and the rate falls rapidly; the microorganisms may also be killed. At very low temperatures enzyme activity is slow, so decay is very slow (this is why a fridge keeps food fresh longer).

bullets: Compost heaps are kept moist but not waterlogged, and turned to add oxygen.
A heap may heat up because microbial respiration releases energy (heat).
Chopping waste increases the surface area for decomposers.
Compost = natural fertiliser, a way of recycling garden and kitchen waste, and it avoids sending waste to landfill.
Aerobic decay: organic matter + oxygen --> carbon dioxide + water + energy (heat), with mineral ions released.
Using compost returns nutrients to the soil in a way that is cheaper and more sustainable than buying artificial fertiliser.
core.p: Gardeners and farmers use decay to make **compost**, which is decayed organic matter such as grass cuttings, vegetable waste and manure. Compost is used as a **natural fertiliser** for growing plants, because decay releases mineral ions and improves soil structure. They try to provide the best conditions for decay: warmth, moisture, a supply of air by turning the heap and small pieces of material. Under these conditions the decomposers respire aerobically and break the material down quickly.

bullets: **Anaerobic**: without oxygen. Decay under anaerobic conditions makes methane.
A biogas generator is a sealed container (digester) into which waste is placed with anaerobic microorganisms; the gas is collected.
Biogas can be burned for heating, cooking or electricity, a **renewable** fuel source because waste is constantly produced.
Large-scale biogas generators and small-scale ones in villages in developing countries both exist.
Methane is also a **greenhouse gas**, so it should be collected and used rather than released.
Temperature affects the generator: it works best when kept warm so that the microorganisms work quickly, and it may need to be kept free of oxygen.
core.p: If there is no oxygen, for example in waterlogged soil or sealed containers, decay is carried out by **anaerobic** microorganisms. They produce **methane gas** instead of just carbon dioxide. Methane is a fuel and can be burned to release energy. **Biogas generators** are used to produce methane (biogas) from waste, such as manure, sewage and plant waste, by anaerobic decay. The gas can be used as a fuel for cooking, heating and generating electricity, and the leftover material can be used as fertiliser.

bullets: **Independent variable**: temperature of the milk mixture (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 degrees C), controlled using water baths.
**Dependent variable**: the time taken for the pH to change to a set value (e.g. the indicator changing colour), or the pH measured at set times with a pH meter or universal indicator.

**Control variables**: volume and type of milk, concentration and volume of lipase (or bacteria), volume of sodium carbonate solution, volume and type of indicator, size and type of container, time left to reach the temperature.
**Rate of decay** = 1 / time taken (or 1000 / time to give larger numbers); a shorter time means a faster rate.

Typical method (with lipase and phenolphthalein): add measured volumes of milk, sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein to a test tube (the mixture is pink because it is alkaline); put the tube and a separate tube of lipase in a water bath at the chosen temperature for several minutes; add the lipase, start the stopwatch, and stir; record the time for the pink colour to disappear.
Repeat at each temperature, calculate a **mean**, and identify and exclude **anomalies**.
Use a thermometer to check the water bath temperature; keep the temperature steady by topping up with hot or cold water.
core.h: Required practical: the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk (Biology only)
core.p: This required practical (**Biology/triple only**) investigates how temperature affects the **rate of decay** of fresh milk by measuring the **change in pH**. As milk decays, microorganisms and enzymes such as lipase break down its fats and sugars to **acids** (fatty acids and lactic acid), so the **pH falls**. The faster the decay, the faster the pH falls. By measuring how long it takes the pH to drop at different temperatures, you can compare rates of decay.

bullets: Choose the correct graph: line graph or curve of best fit since temperature is a continuous variable.
Describe the pattern with data: 'the time taken falls from X s at 20 degrees C to Y s at 40 degrees C'.
Explain: higher temperature --> more kinetic energy --> more collisions --> faster enzyme and microbial activity; at high temperature the enzymes denature.
Sources of error: temperature of the water bath drifting, judging the colour change by eye (subjective), delay in starting the stopwatch, differing starting mix.
Improvements: use a **pH meter** or data logger, use more temperatures near the optimum, repeat more, keep tubes in the bath for equal time before mixing.
If the milk is left at room temperature and bacteria are the decomposers, remember that microbes can be harmful, so do not incubate cultures above about 25-30 degrees C in school unless instructed.
core.p: You must be able to plot the results, describe the pattern, explain it with enzyme theory and evaluate the method. Plot **mean rate of decay** (or time) on the y axis against temperature on the x axis and draw a smooth curve of best fit, because the data is continuous. Expect the rate to rise to a maximum and then fall at the highest temperatures. Explain the rise using increased collisions and activity, and the fall by denaturation. Evaluate the quality of the data using repeats, anomalies and the precision of the measurements.

bullets: Wear eye protection (goggles) and tie back long hair.
Hot water baths: risk of scalds; carry water carefully, use a stable base and avoid very hot water.
If microorganisms are involved, wash hands, disinfect the bench afterwards and do not incubate at body temperature.
Dispose of milk and cultures properly; do not taste any mixture.
Spills on the floor: mop up immediately to prevent slipping.
State the **precaution** with the hazard: e.g. 'Sodium carbonate is an irritant, so wear goggles and wash off any splashes with water.'
core.h: Required practical: safety and risk assessment
core.p: A risk assessment identifies each hazard, the harm it could cause and how to reduce the risk. Use the language of the mark scheme: a hazard is something that could cause harm, and the risk is the chance that it will. For this practical the chemicals include sodium carbonate, which is an irritant, phenolphthalein (usually in an alcohol solution, so keep away from flames and follow the CLEAPSS hazard card), and lipase, an enzyme that can irritate the skin and eyes.

bullets: Rate = 1 / time (units per second), so time of 50 s gives rate 0.02 per s, or 20 per 1000 s.
The optimum temperature is where the rate is highest (shortest time).
Describe in three parts: the trend at low temperature, the peak, then the change at high temperature.
Use data from the table or graph in the answer, including units.
A rate of zero at a very high temperature suggests the enzymes were denatured and the microorganisms killed.
Compare rates using ratios, e.g. 'the rate at 40 degrees C was twice the rate at 30 degrees C'.
core.h: Interpreting rate of decay data and graphs
core.p: Questions on this topic often give a table or graph of results and ask you to calculate the rate, describe the trend or suggest the optimum. Read the axes and units first. A shorter time for the colour change means a faster rate, so a graph of time against temperature is the shape of a 'U' (inverted), while a graph of rate (1/time) against temperature is a hill. Be careful not to say that a higher number means a higher rate unless the quantity measured is a rate.

bullets: Fridge: low temperature slows microbial growth but does not kill them.
Freezer: very low temperature almost stops enzyme action.
Canning: food is heated to kill microbes and then sealed to stop new ones entering.
Drying, salting and sugar syrup: remove available water by osmosis, so microbes cannot grow.
Vacuum packing and sealed cans: remove oxygen so aerobic decomposers cannot respire.
Always link your answer to the factor involved: temperature, water, oxygen, or pH.
core.p: Because food is decayed by microorganisms, many methods of preserving food work by removing the conditions decomposers need. **Cooling or freezing** slows enzyme activity; **heating** (canning, pasteurising) kills microbes; **drying** removes water; **salting, pickling and adding sugar** remove water or lower the pH so microbes cannot grow; **vacuum packing** removes oxygen. This link to the rate-of-decay factors is a common application question.

bullets: Decay in the carbon cycle: dead organisms and waste are broken down; CO2 returned.
Decay and enzymes: extracellular enzymes digest the dead material.
Decay and food chains: biomass in waste and dead organisms is not lost but recycled.
Decay and agriculture: compost and manure as natural fertilisers.
Decay and energy resources: biogas from anaerobic decay as a fuel.
Decay and practical skills: planning, variables, rate calculations and evaluation.
core.h: Linking decay to the wider course
core.p: Decay connects many topics: the **carbon cycle** (decomposers release CO2 by respiration), **enzymes** (digestion outside the cell, effect of temperature and pH), **food chains and biomass transfer** (decomposers break down the biomass that is not passed on), **ecosystems and sustainability** (compost and biogas), and **investigations** (variables, rate calculations, graphs). Using these links in 6-mark answers helps show depth of understanding.

exam: **Command words**: 'State' (1 fact), 'Describe' (give features/pattern), 'Explain' (reasons using 'because'), 'Suggest' (apply knowledge), 'Evaluate' (strengths, weaknesses, conclusion).
For 'conditions for fast decay' always give three: **warm, moist, plenty of oxygen** (and small pieces), and say why (enzymes and microbes work best).
For explaining a drop in rate at high temperature: 'the enzymes are denatured; the active site changes shape; the substrate no longer fits'.

For 'describe the method' (required practical, 4-6 marks) give the order: measure volumes, set water bath temperature, allow to reach temperature, mix and start timer, record time for colour change, repeat, mean.
Variables: name the independent (temperature), dependent (time for pH/colour change) and at least two controls with quantities, e.g. 'same volume of milk, 5 cm3'.
For calculations show the formula: rate = 1 / time; give units (per second or s-1).
Biogas / compost questions: give the **benefit** (natural fertiliser, renewable fuel) and the **conditions** (oxygen for compost; no oxygen for biogas).
Graphs: label axes with quantity and unit, choose a sensible scale, plot accurately, draw a smooth curve, not a ruled line to each point.
Evaluation: refer to precision (colour change judged by eye), repeats, range of temperatures and the effect of anomalies.
Safety marks: hazard + precaution pairs, e.g. hot water --> risk of scalds --> use a stable bath and handle carefully.
Use 'because' links to turn a description into an explanation and gain explain marks.
Check whether the question is about aerobic or anaerobic decay and answer with the right gas.

mistakes.r: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi found in soil, water and on all dead matter, including food such as milk.
mistakes.w: Decomposers are only found in the soil.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are not alive; they are denatured because the shape of the active site changes.
mistakes.w: Enzymes are killed at high temperature.

mistakes.r: Decay is fastest at the optimum temperature; above it enzymes denature and microbes die, so the rate falls.
mistakes.w: Decay is fastest at the highest temperature.

mistakes.r: Rate is 1 / time. A shorter time means a faster rate.
mistakes.w: The rate of decay is the time taken.

mistakes.r: They are broken down because decomposers secrete enzymes and respire, which needs warmth, water and oxygen.
mistakes.w: Dead things rot because they are old.

mistakes.r: Anaerobic decay produces methane; aerobic decay produces carbon dioxide.
mistakes.w: Anaerobic decay produces carbon dioxide only.

mistakes.r: As milk decays, acids (fatty acids, lactic acid) form so the pH falls.
mistakes.w: The pH rises as milk goes off.

mistakes.r: Keep volume, concentrations, time in the bath and equipment the same to make it a fair test.
mistakes.w: Changing temperature is the only variable; I need not control anything else.

summary: You must know how decomposers break down dead material and waste, the conditions that give the fastest rate of decay (warm, moist, plenty of oxygen), how compost and biogas generators make use of decay (Biology only), and how to carry out and evaluate the required practical on the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk by measuring pH change. It matters because decay recycles carbon and mineral ions and links to enzymes, the carbon cycle and practical skills.

terms.d: The breakdown of dead organisms and waste by decomposers into simpler substances.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead plants and animals and waste.
How quickly dead material is broken down; measured as 1 / time for a chosen change.
Needing or using oxygen; aerobic decay gives carbon dioxide and water.
Without oxygen; anaerobic decay produces methane.
Decayed organic matter such as plant waste and manure, used as a natural fertiliser.
A container in which anaerobic decay of waste produces methane gas to be used as a fuel.
A gas produced by anaerobic decay, used as a fuel; also a greenhouse gas.
Ions such as nitrate, phosphate and magnesium released by decay and taken up by plant roots.
A biological catalyst, a protein that speeds up reactions without being used up.
The change in shape of the active site of an enzyme at high temperature or extreme pH so that the substrate no longer fits.
The temperature at which the rate of reaction is highest.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.
The variable that is changed by the investigator.
A variable that is kept the same so that it does not affect the results.
A result that does not fit the pattern and is excluded when calculating a mean.
A substance added to soil to provide mineral ions for plant growth.

worked.ans: Rates are 2.5 and 10 (units 1000/s). The rate at 40 degrees C is 4 times the rate at 20 degrees C.
worked.q: A student measured the time taken for the pink colour to disappear in milk, sodium carbonate, phenolphthalein and lipase at different temperatures. At 20 degrees C the time was 400 s, at 40 degrees C it was 100 s. Calculate the rate (1000 / time) at each temperature and compare them. (3 marks)
steps: Ratio = 10 / 2.5 = 4, so the rate is four times faster at 40 degrees C (1).

worked.ans: The enzymes denature because the active site changes shape and the substrate can no longer fit; microorganisms may also die, so the rate falls.
worked.q: Explain why the rate of decay of milk decreases at 70 degrees C compared with 40 degrees C. (3 marks)
steps: At high temperature the enzymes in the decomposers (and the lipase) are denatured (1).
The shape of the active site changes so the substrate no longer fits (1).
Microorganisms may also be killed, so less breakdown occurs (1).

worked.ans: A full-mark answer states the independent variable (temperature), dependent variable (time for colour change), control variables, the method order, repeats and mean, and a safety precaution.
worked.q: Describe how you would investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk. (6 marks)
steps: Use a measuring cylinder to add 5 cm3 milk, 5 cm3 sodium carbonate solution and a few drops of phenolphthalein to a test tube (the mixture is pink).
Place the tube and a separate tube of lipase solution in a water bath at 20 degrees C for 5 minutes; check the temperature with a thermometer.
Add 1 cm3 lipase, start the stopwatch, stir, and record the time for the pink colour to disappear.
Repeat at 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees C, keeping volumes, concentrations and equilibration time the same (control variables).
Repeat each temperature three times and calculate a mean; exclude anomalies.
Calculate rate = 1 / time and plot rate against temperature; take safety precautions: wear goggles, handle hot water carefully.
